evaluated.name: Gross-profit yield net of obligations
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(re, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Deep value measured in gross profit rather than raw sales already screens out unprofitable revenue, and it converts into realized returns only for firms whose accumulated retained earnings exceed their debt obligations; cheap firms with retained-earnings deficits financed by debt are the archetypal value trap.
evaluated.reasoning: The valuation leg is gross profit to price, an interaction of sales-to-price with the gross margin, so cheapness is defined only over profitable sales instead of stacking a separate profitability anomaly. The conditioning leg is one coherent solvency construct, retained earnings net of total debt scaled by assets, and it enters multiplicatively so that leveraged retained-deficit firms receive near-zero exposure regardless of how cheap they look, which removes the equal-weight additive claim the critic rejected.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Depreciation-charge cheapness gap
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ebitda, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Two firms can look equally cheap on EBITDA-to-price, but the one whose cheapness survives the depreciation charge owns economically durable earnings, while the one whose EBITDA yield evaporates after capital consumption is cheap only because maintenance capital expenditure will absorb the cash flow.
evaluated.reasoning: The rank difference is deliberately factor-balanced: both legs are populated by firms with similar headline EBITDA yields, so the spread strips out the value factor and prices only the quality of the cheapness, the exact structural fix for gen-0's zero FF5 alpha. Economically it operationalizes the capital-intensity trap using depreciation as the accounting measure of consumed capital, a channel untested so far in this archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidity-signed sales yield
evaluated.expression: SUB(MUL(RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), INDICATOR(RATIO(act, lct), 1.5)), MUL(RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(act, lct)), -1.5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among deep-value firms identified by high sales-to-price, near-term liquidity determines the outcome: those with current assets comfortably covering current liabilities are cheap and solvent, while those without the coverage face refinancing pressure that makes the cheapness rational.
evaluated.reasoning: The sign flip at a current ratio of 1.5 makes both the long and short legs deep-value stocks, so the spread is a within-value liquidity contrast whose HML loading largely cancels, leaving the interaction to be priced as alpha. Sales-to-price is the right value leg here because it remains defined for firms with temporarily negative earnings, which is precisely the population where the liquidity distinction between trap and bargain is economically decisive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheapness with stable cost structure
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(VOL(RATIO(cogs, sale), 5)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm whose cost-of-goods-to-sales ratio has been stable for five years has a controllable cost structure and can absorb a demand shock, whereas equally cheap firms with an erratic cost ratio have high operating leverage and unstable unit economics, which is what turns a low multiple into a trap.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the product of signed z-scores with MIN removes the double-negative pathology entirely: a firm scores highly only if it is simultaneously cheap and operationally stable, and expensive firms with unstable costs now sit in the short leg where the hypothesis places them. The quality channel is cost-ratio stability rather than a profitability level, so this tests operating-leverage fragility rather than re-running the heavily published value-times-gross-profitability pairing.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Within-industry margin-signed value
evaluated.expression: SUB(MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at)), 0)), MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), INDICATOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at))), 0)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Within an industry, a firm trading cheap relative to peers while earning above-peer gross profitability is being mispriced, while an equally peer-cheap firm earning below-peer profitability is losing the competitive contest and its discount is warranted.
evaluated.reasoning: The z-score product is replaced by an explicit two-cell sign flip so the long and short legs are both peer-cheap stocks that differ only in whether profitability beats the industry norm, which implements the stated logic exactly and keeps the HML loading of the two legs similar so any spread shows up as FF5 alpha. Industry demeaning is no longer the mechanism but the measurement convention for both the value and quality legs, making the comparison a competitive-position test rather than a neutralization variant.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Deleveraging-signed book-to-market
evaluated.expression: SUB(MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), INDICATOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1)), 0)), MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), INDICATOR(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), 0)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What separates a recovering cheap firm from a deteriorating one is the direction of its obligation burden: cheap firms that reduced total liabilities relative to assets over the past year are repairing the balance sheet the market is discounting, while cheap firms adding liabilities are funding losses and the discount is rational.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the static balance-sheet-strength level that overlapped the archive's retained-earnings-net-of-debt leg and the Piotroski-style screen, and instead conditions on the flow of liabilities, which is a forward-looking state change rather than a distress level. The sign flip makes both legs high-book-to-market stocks so the spread is a within-value deleveraging contrast, and it fixes the earlier defect in which expensive liability-heavy firms scored positive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Own-history cheapness signed by margin trend
evaluated.expression: SUB(MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), INDICATOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 5), 0)), MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), INDICATOR(NEG(TREND(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 5)), 0)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm sitting near the top of its own five-year book-to-market range is being ignored if its gross margin is simultaneously improving, but the same persistent cheapness with an eroding margin is the market correctly pricing competitive decay.
evaluated.reasoning: The two-cell logic is now implemented literally: own-history cheapness receives a positive loading when the five-year margin trend is up and an equal negative loading when it is down, so the low-cheapness/eroding-margin cell no longer scores at the top as it did under the z-score product. Because both legs are drawn from firms cheap relative to their own history rather than to the cross-section, the spread's HML exposure is muted and the surviving return should register as abnormal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidation-backed value gap
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Two firms equally cheap on book value differ sharply in the realizability of that book value: when current assets alone exceed all liabilities, the discount is protected by near-cash resources, whereas book value consisting of depreciated fixed and intangible assets can evaporate before any revaluation occurs.
evaluated.reasoning: The gap between net-current-asset cheapness and total-book cheapness holds market capitalization fixed across both legs, isolating asset quality rather than the value factor, and it operationalizes the classic Graham solvency-backed discount using balance-sheet quality items (act, lt). Unlike the earlier liquidity-signed sales yield with its arbitrary 1.5 current-ratio cut, the conditioning here is continuous and expressed in the same price-scaled units as the value leg, avoiding the mass-at-zero problem that flattened that signal's alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EBITDA yield surviving capital consumption
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ebitda, dp), ebitda), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A low EBITDA multiple is real cheapness only when most of that EBITDA survives the depreciation charge; when depreciation consumes the majority of EBITDA, the apparent yield is committed to replacing worn-out capacity and cannot accrue to shareholders.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-1 depreciation gap produced a strong FF5 alpha but a wrong-signed FMB slope precisely because, as the critic noted, it collapsed into depreciation-to-market-cap, a capital-intensity characteristic rather than a conditional statement. Making the quality leg scale-free — the fraction of EBITDA left after depreciation — removes the price scaling from the conditioner so the signal can only score highly when cheapness and capital-charge coverage coincide, which should align the cross-sectional slope with the portfolio alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: De-rating without cost deterioration
evaluated.expression: SUB(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(cogs, revt), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: A stock that sits at the cheap extreme of its own five-year valuation range while its cost-of-goods-to-revenue ratio is near the low end of its own five-year range has de-rated without any operating deterioration, which is mispricing; when the de-rating is accompanied by the firm's worst-ever cost ratio, the market is correctly capitalizing margin erosion.
evaluated.reasoning: Both legs are within-firm time-series percentiles rather than cross-sectional levels, so the signal cannot collapse into the retained-earnings/book-to-market decomposition or any other published cross-sectional ratio, and its HML and RMW loadings are muted because a firm can appear in either leg regardless of its level of cheapness or profitability. The economic content is a genuine interaction: identical valuation percentiles receive opposite scores depending on whether unit costs have simultaneously moved to a historical extreme.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Equity-funded sales yield
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(MUL(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(SUB(at, lt), at)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: A high sales-to-price ratio manufactured by financing the operating base with liabilities is not cheapness but leverage; only the revenue supported by equity-funded assets represents a discount available to shareholders, so scaling the sales yield by the equity share of the asset base separates real bargains from levered traps.
evaluated.reasoning: The two legs have different denominators (market value and total assets), so unlike the flagged version the product does not reduce to an ordering of one accounting item against another and is not a restatement of gross profitability or gross-profits-to-market. Economically it is a re-definition of the multiple rather than a screen bolted onto it: a deep-value firm with liabilities equal to most of its assets is pushed toward the middle of the distribution instead of the long leg, which is exactly the trap the theme asks us to remove.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with deteriorating near-term liquidity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(lct, act), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The trap side of the interaction is driven by funding pressure in motion: cheap firms whose current liabilities are rising relative to current assets are being forced to finance operations with short-dated claims, and this deterioration, not the static level of leverage, predicts continued underperformance.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the MIN-of-z-scores template with a product of ranks removes the ambiguity the critic identified, since the low end is now unambiguously expensive-or-improving firms rather than a mixture, and the negative expected slope no longer contradicts the value premium because the conditioner is a deterioration flow rather than a distress level. This isolates the short leg of the theme using a channel — the direction of short-term liquidity change — that no prior archive signal has tested.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Affordable dividend yield gap
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(dvc, SUB(sale, cogs))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high dividend yield is credible evidence of earnings quality only when the payout consumes a small fraction of gross profit; firms delivering a large yield out of a small share of their gross profit have distributable, verified earnings, while firms whose dividend absorbs most of gross profit are yielding on borrowed time.
evaluated.reasoning: The two ranks share a numerator but have economically different denominators — market value versus gross profit — so the gap measures payout affordability given the yield rather than reducing to accruals or any single published characteristic, which was the defect in the flagged working-capital version. Cash dividends are the one quality signal management cannot accrue, so pairing yield with gross-profit coverage tests a verification mechanism absent from the archive so far.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Solvency-covered EBIT yield
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ebitda, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ebitda, dp), ADD(ADD(dltt, dlc), lct)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A low multiple on operating profit measured after the depreciation charge is genuine cheapness only when that same operating profit is large relative to the firm's total claims; when a cheap EBIT yield comes with obligations many times operating profit, the discount is compensation for a real probability that creditors capture the recovery.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the diagnosis-driven refinement of the archive's best joint performer: the unstable (ebitda-dp)/ebitda conditioner, which flips sign for negative-EBITDA firms, is replaced by a monotone coverage ratio, and the value leg becomes EBIT yield so both legs share the same well-defined numerator. The conditioner is scale-free and denominated in claims rather than price, so it adds information HML and CMA cannot span while the value leg preserves the cross-sectional slope.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Supplier-financed deep value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), lt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Not all leverage is distress: a deep-value firm whose liabilities are mostly trade credit and other operating current liabilities rather than financial debt is being financed by suppliers who monitor it daily and continue to extend terms, whereas the same cheapness funded by borrowings is a trap because lenders can accelerate.
evaluated.reasoning: The liability *composition* channel is untested in the archive, which has only examined liability levels and changes, and it flips the usual interpretation of a leveraged value stock by distinguishing renewable operating float from contractual debt. Both the value leg (sales-to-price, defined for loss makers) and the scale-free composition leg are orthogonal to FF5's leverage-blind factors, so the conjunction can produce alpha rather than a repackaged HML tilt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with liquid asset backing
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Book cheapness is trustworthy when current assets alone exceed all liabilities, because the discount is then backed by near-cash resources rather than by depreciated fixed assets that can be written down before any revaluation.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-2 liquidation gap earned a 3.9% alpha but a negative FMB slope and zero Sharpe, which diagnoses it as an asset-composition bet that goes long asset-light firms and abandons cheapness entirely; scaling net liquid assets by total assets instead of by market value, and requiring cheapness jointly through MIN, restores the value tilt that drives the cross-sectional slope while keeping the solvency-backing content that produced the alpha. This is the specific structural repair the metric disagreement calls for, not a re-scaling for its own sake.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Obligation-covered dividend yield
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dvc), lct)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high dividend yield is verified earnings quality only if cash flow left after paying the dividend still covers near-term obligations; firms paying large yields while retaining nothing against current liabilities are pre-cut yields, the classic trap.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-2 dividend affordability gap was the second design with both statistics positive, and this changes its economic content rather than its cosmetics: coverage is measured against current liabilities using post-dividend cash flow, so it tests whether the payout is sustainable against claims rather than merely small relative to gross profit. Cash dividends are the one quality signal that cannot be accrued, which is why this channel plausibly carries information beyond RMW.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with tightening working capital
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), ZSCORE(TS_RANK(RATIO(revt, act), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among deep-value firms, those running their receivables and inventory at the most productive level of their own five-year history are operationally tightening and their discount is a mispricing, while equally cheap firms whose current assets are at their least productive level are accumulating unsold inventory and uncollected receivables, the operating signature of a value trap.
evaluated.reasoning: The conditioner is now a within-firm five-year percentile of current-asset turnover rather than its cross-sectional level, so it is not the published DuPont efficiency characteristic and it cannot be arbitraged by industry-level asset-intensity differences: a distributor and a software firm are each judged against their own norm. Bounding the conditioner in [0,1] before standardizing also fixes the tail-domination problem of the raw product, so the score genuinely requires the conjunction of cheapness and improving working-capital productivity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Self-funding value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Book cheapness converts into shareholder return only when the firm generates cash beyond the capital it consumes and that surplus is large relative to everything it owes; a cheap firm whose post-maintenance cash flow is negligible against its liabilities depends on creditors and capital markets for survival, which is why its discount persists.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the standalone free-cash-flow yield with a genuine interaction: the depreciation-adjusted cash surplus is deflated by total liabilities rather than by price, so it is a scale-free solvency conditioner that cannot be a value ratio in disguise, and the cheapness leg supplies the valuation theme separately. Pairing it with the accepted accrual-based EBIT coverage signal makes the batch informative, since the two differ precisely in whether the coverage numerator is cash after capital maintenance or accounting operating profit.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Refinancing-gap conditioned value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(dlc, act)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What kills value stocks is not the level of debt but its timing: a cheap firm whose debt coming due within a year is small relative to its liquid assets controls its own destiny, whereas a cheap firm whose maturing debt exceeds its current assets must refinance into the same pessimism that made it cheap.
evaluated.reasoning: Debt *maturity* structure is an untested channel in this archive, which has examined leverage levels, leverage changes and liability composition but never the near-term rollover requirement against liquid resources. It is economically distinct from total-liability coverage because two firms with identical lt/at can differ entirely in whether creditors can force the issue this year, and it uses only balance-sheet items, preserving the coverage that cash-flow-based conditioners destroyed.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with accumulating retained earnings
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), ZSCORE(TREND(RATIO(re, at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm that has been steadily building retained earnings relative to its asset base is compounding value the market is ignoring, whereas a cheap firm whose retained earnings are eroding is financing losses out of accumulated capital and its discount is a forecast of further erosion.
evaluated.reasoning: The conditioner is the five-year trend in earned equity, a slow-moving accumulation state rather than a level, so it is not the published retained-earnings-to-market decomposition and it is not a single-year profitability measure that RMW would span. It also tests the direction opposite to the archive's failed deleveraging conditioner: whether the informative fundamental flow for value stocks is on the earned-equity side rather than the liability side.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Gross profit yield on total claims
evaluated.expression: RANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness should be measured against everything the firm owes, not only against its equity: a firm generating large gross profit per dollar of combined market equity and total liabilities is genuinely inexpensive, whereas a firm that looks cheap on equity only because liabilities have grown to dominate its claim structure is a trap priced correctly.
evaluated.reasoning: The quality theme enters through the denominator rather than as a bolted-on screen, so a levered value stock is mechanically reclassified as expensive instead of being flagged by a separate conditioner — a different construction from the archive's equity-funded sales yield, which multiplied a value ratio by an equity-share factor and left the multiple itself untouched. It abandons the MIN template and the liquidity conditioner family entirely, uses only long-history income-statement and balance-sheet items, and should retain the strong cross-sectional slope of gross-profit-based value legs while shedding part of the HML loading because liability-heavy cheap firms leave the long leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with consumed asset base
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(dp, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high depreciation charge relative to assets means the reported asset base is old and carried well below replacement cost, so a firm that is cheap on stated book value while depreciating heavily is even cheaper on economic book value — the accounting understatement is the source of the mispricing rather than a capital treadmill.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's depreciation signals are internally contradictory — the gap version went long *low* depreciation and earned a 3.6% alpha but a significantly negative cross-sectional slope — which means the cross-section actually rewards high depreciation intensity, and this proposal is the orientation that reconciles slope and story instead of inheriting the conflicted one. It also removes the redundancy the critic identified, since the conditioner is now deliberately correlated with fixed-asset intensity rather than being paired with a liquidity screen that mechanically requires the opposite.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Distribution-verified profit yield
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(MA(dvc, 3), lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash actually paid out over several years, measured against what the firm owes, is a verification that reported profits are real and unencumbered; a cheap firm distributing meaningful cash relative to its obligations is mispriced, while a cheap firm distributing nothing against heavy obligations has already told investors its profits are committed to creditors.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the 0-to-5 payment count with three-year average dividends scaled by total liabilities makes the conditioner continuous across payers and removes the degenerate tied floor that would have turned the previous version into a payer/non-payer screen, and using RANK rather than MIN means non-payers are ordered among themselves by the value leg instead of being dumped into one indistinguishable short bucket. Scaling the payout by liabilities rather than by price or earnings keeps the conditioner scale-free and economically distinct from dividend yield, which is a valuation variable in its own right.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with volatile cost structure
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(VOL(RATIO(cogs, revt), 5), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among value stocks the mispricing lives with operating leverage, not against it: a cheap firm whose cost-to-revenue ratio swings widely has earnings that respond convexly to any demand recovery, and the market systematically underprices that convexity, while a cheap firm with a placid cost structure is stably mediocre and its low multiple is deserved.
evaluated.reasoning: This is an evidence-driven reversal rather than a new guess: the archive's Cheapness with stable cost structure used exactly the opposite orientation and produced a significantly *negative* FF5 alpha (-2.0%, t = -2.49) alongside a positive slope, which is direct information that within cheap firms the high-cost-volatility side is where abnormal return sits. Testing the flipped conditioner with a coherent operating-leverage story converts a prior failure into a signed prediction, and it is the only proposal in this set whose quality channel is a second moment rather than a level or a flow.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Claims-based profit yield free of fixed capital
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), NEG(RATIO(SUB(at, act), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Two separate things make a cheap firm a genuine bargain rather than a trap: its gross profit must be large relative to every claim on the enterprise, and its market value must not be merely a claim on depreciating plant. Firms that satisfy both are underpriced operating franchises; asset-heavy firms priced off fixed capital are the traps.
evaluated.reasoning: This fuses the archive's best cross-sectional leg (gross profit to market equity plus liabilities: FMB 4.32, Sharpe 0.50) with the characteristic algebraically responsible for both large FF5 alphas (non-current assets scaled by price, entering negatively), so it is a deliberate consolidation of two empirically separated sources of evidence rather than a new guess. SUMRANK equalizes the two channels' influence and keeps the composite robust to the heavy tails of price-scaled fixed assets.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquid-backed claims profit yield
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm cheap on gross profit relative to all claims is mispriced only if its balance sheet can survive the wait; requiring current assets to cover total liabilities screens out the leveraged, illiquid names whose discount is compensation for a real chance of impairment.
evaluated.reasoning: This upgrades the value leg of the archive's only both-positive signal (Cheap with liquid asset backing: FMB 3.97, alpha +2.2%, t 1.92) from book-to-market — which drags in the HML loading responsible for the negative alphas elsewhere — to the claims-based gross profit yield, holding the conditioner fixed so the comparison isolates exactly one design choice with a strong prior of improving both metrics. Because the value leg already penalizes liabilities in its denominator, the conjunction should concentrate on profitable, solvent, cheap firms instead of on levered deep value.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap and asset-light on the balance sheet
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(at, act), at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm cheap on gross profit relative to all claims is mispriced when little of its balance sheet is tied up in non-current assets, because plant and equipment both pre-commit future cash to replacement and are the assets most likely to be impaired before the discount closes.
evaluated.reasoning: Scaling non-current assets by total assets instead of by market equity removes the price term from the conditioner, so the two legs no longer move mechanically against each other and the MIN can no longer be pinned to the fixed-capital leg for exactly the cheap firms of interest — the flaw that made the earlier version a rescaled liquidation gap. With the value leg identical to the accepted liquidity-conditioned proposal, this is now a clean horse race between asset-side solvency and asset-side capital intensity as the carrier of the archive's positive alphas.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with productive fixed capital
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), SUB(at, act))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital intensity is not itself a defect — idle capital is. A cheap firm that wrings a large gross profit out of each dollar of plant is running a productive franchise the market is discounting, while an equally cheap firm whose plant generates little profit is holding stranded capacity, which is the asset-side definition of a value trap.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces a one-term numerator tweak of an evaluated expression with a different economic construct, fixed-capital productivity, which is conceptually distinct from the capital-intensity level that the archive's alphas load on: an asset-heavy firm can score highly here if its plant earns, whereas the intensity channel would reject it outright. Ranking both legs before multiplying avoids the tail-domination problem of raw products, and pairing productivity with the claims-based value leg keeps the batch comparable across conditioners.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Trade-float discount gap
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that look expensive when all liabilities are treated as claims but cheap once only net financial debt is counted are financed by renewable supplier float rather than by hard obligations; the market discounts them as if payables were debt, and that confusion is the mispricing.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than substituting one published multiple for another, the signal is the *difference* between two claim definitions of the same profit stream, so it isolates precisely the unsettled economic question — whether operating liabilities are dangerous claims or benign float — and it has the factor-balanced gap structure that produced the archive's only alphas above t = 3, since both legs share a numerator and a market-equity term. The long leg is payables-financed firms with little net debt, which is a different population from the supplier-composition screen already tested and is not spanned by any FF5 factor.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Operating-accrual-clean claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness is trustworthy when reported profits are not being manufactured by expanding receivables and inventory: a cheap firm whose operating working capital, measured net of cash and short-term borrowing, is not outrunning its depreciation charge is genuinely earning, while one accumulating operating accruals is booking profits it has not collected.
evaluated.reasoning: The conditioner now implements the accrual definition the hypothesis actually requires — cash is netted out of current assets and short-term debt out of current liabilities, so hoarding cash is no longer scored as poor accrual quality and borrowing short is no longer rewarded. Computing accruals from the balance sheet also preserves the 0.12+ coverage that every oancf-based design destroyed, letting the archive finally evaluate the earnings-quality channel named in the theme statement, interacted with the claims-based value leg rather than in isolation.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Solvency and productivity conditioned claims yield
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), SUB(at, act)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness on gross profit relative to all claims converts into return when the firm is both able to survive the wait (current assets covering liabilities) and running its fixed capital productively; these are separate defects — a liquid firm with idle plant and an illiquid firm with productive plant are both traps for different reasons.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's two best conditioners deliver alphas of 4.5% and 3.4% through economically different channels, and combining them as a SUMRANK composite before the conjunction avoids the long-leg thinning and instability that a triple-nested MIN would cause. If this beats both parents on alpha and t-statistic the two quality defects are genuinely independent; if it lands between them they are proxies for the same asset-composition effect, which is the key structural question for the final generations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Peer-relative capital productivity value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), SUB(at, act)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Gross profit per dollar of fixed capital is set largely by industry technology, so the informative signal is a cheap firm whose plant earns more than its own peers' plant, not one that happens to operate in an intrinsically asset-light sector.
evaluated.reasoning: The productivity conditioner is the most likely of the working channels to be a sector tilt — utilities and heavy manufacturers sit permanently at the bottom — and industry-demeaning only that leg is the sharpest test of whether the 3.4% alpha is firm-level mispricing or sector composition. This matters for the final generations because a sector-driven result would argue for neutralizing the conditioner, while a surviving alpha would justify pushing the productivity channel harder.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Net-debt claims yield with liquid backing
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che))), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Only net financial debt is a hard claim that can force a cheap firm into distress, so measuring cheapness against market equity plus net debt — while separately requiring liquid backing — should identify mispricing more cleanly than treating renewable trade payables as claims.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive left the claim-definition question genuinely unresolved: total liabilities in the denominator produced the best joint result, yet the trade-float gap showed a 2.4% alpha specifically for firms whose payables are large relative to net debt, and the two findings cannot both be fully right. Holding the conditioner fixed and changing only the claim definition inside the winning recipe settles which liabilities make cheapness dangerous, and it also removes the double liability penalty the critic identified in the current best signal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Float-financed claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), lt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheap, profitable firms the safe ones are those whose obligations are mostly supplier and operating liabilities rather than borrowings, because trade creditors monitor continuously and roll their exposure while lenders can accelerate at exactly the wrong moment.
evaluated.reasoning: The liability-composition channel produced a strong slope but null alpha when paired with a raw sales-yield value leg in gen 3, whereas the same economics priced as a valuation gap produced a 2.4% alpha with a null slope in gen 5 — pairing it with the value leg now known to carry the cross-sectional signal is the natural test of whether both halves can be obtained at once. It also diversifies the batch away from asset-side conditioners toward the liability side, so the generation as a whole covers both sources of trap risk.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with improving capital utilization
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), SUB(at, act)), 5), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What distinguishes a mispriced cheap firm from a trap is not only how productive its plant is today but whether that productivity is rising: a cheap firm extracting steadily more gross profit from the same fixed capital base is filling capacity that the market still prices as idle, whereas a cheap firm with falling capital productivity is losing share and its discount will keep widening.
evaluated.reasoning: This changes the economic content rather than the operator: the archive established that the *level* of fixed-capital productivity carries alpha, and the untested question is whether the market misprices the level or the direction of change, which is a different behavioural claim about slow updating of capacity expectations. The five-year trend is genuinely slow-moving and orthogonal to the level for many firms — a low-productivity plant can be improving fast — so the result is informative regardless of sign and cannot be replicated by the accepted Signal 1's static composite.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Profit yield on illiquid claim base
evaluated.expression: RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(lt, act))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically relevant capital a buyer must fund is market equity plus the liabilities that current assets cannot already extinguish; pricing gross profit against that net, illiquid claim base means a firm whose receivables, inventory and cash already offset its obligations is recognised as cheap, while a firm whose liabilities exceed its liquid resources is correctly recognised as expensive.
evaluated.reasoning: The flow-plus-stock addition that made the earlier version arbitrarily weighted is removed: the numerator is now purely a flow and the balance-sheet quality information enters as a deduction inside the denominator, so all terms in the claim base are stocks and no implicit capitalization multiple is assumed. It is distinct from gross-profits-to-enterprise-value, which nets only cash, and it makes the solvency conditioner that produced the archive's 4.5% alpha part of the multiple itself; the rare cases where current assets exceed market equity plus liabilities are the deep net-net names and are handled by winsorizing before ranking.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Two-sided balance-sheet quality value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap, profitable firm avoids the trap for two logically separate reasons: its assets are liquid enough to cover its obligations, and the obligations it has are renewable supplier float rather than acceleratable debt. Asset-side capacity and liability-side patience are distinct forms of staying power.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-6 attempt to combine two conditioners paired asset liquidity with capital productivity, which the critic correctly noted are mechanically linked through the same small non-current asset base; pairing asset liquidity with liability *composition* combines channels that were separately alpha-positive (4.5% and 3.0%) and are not driven by the same accounting identity. This is the last remaining plausible route to independent, additive quality information within the winning recipe.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Smoothed earnings power on claims with solvency
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(SUB(sale, cogs), 3), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The cheapness that matters is measured against normal earning power, not against a single year's gross profit: averaging three years of gross profit removes cyclical peaks that make deteriorating firms look cheap and cyclical troughs that hide genuinely cheap franchises.
evaluated.reasoning: Every value leg in this archive has used a single fiscal year, so the timing of the earnings-power measurement is an untested design dimension, and it targets a specific trap mechanism — peak-earnings cheapness — that the balance-sheet conditioners cannot detect. Smoothing should also reduce annual turnover in the long leg, which is the most likely source of incremental improvement in ls_talpha given the alpha magnitude is already established.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Peer-relative claims value with solvency
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Gross-profit multiples differ permanently across industries, so the mispriced firm is the one cheap relative to its own peers, while the solvency requirement remains an absolute standard because creditors do not grade on an industry curve.
evaluated.reasoning: Industry-demeaning the productivity conditioner destroyed its alpha, which showed the conditioner side is a sector effect; the complementary and unanswered question is whether the *value* leg's contribution is within-industry mispricing or a cross-industry multiple tilt, and this signal isolates exactly that by demeaning only the value leg. The answer determines whether the final consolidated signal should be industry-neutral on the valuation dimension, which materially affects the stability of the long-short spread.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Earned-buffer claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(re, lt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The deepest form of staying power is a stock of profits already earned and retained relative to what the firm owes: such a firm has demonstrated over its life that it can fund obligations internally, whereas a cheap firm with an accumulated deficit against heavy liabilities has never demonstrated it and its discount is a distress forecast.
evaluated.reasoning: All the alpha-producing conditioners so far measure current asset or liability composition; retained earnings relative to liabilities is a cumulative, history-based buffer that is conceptually distinct — asset-heavy old firms with decades of retained profit can score highly here while failing every liquidity screen. Because it uses no price term and no flow, it cannot double-count the value leg or the asset-lightness tilt, making it the most genuinely new conditioner class available within the winning recipe.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Two-route value disjunction
evaluated.expression: MAX(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: There are two independent routes by which a stock can be worth more than its price — a large profit stream relative to all claims, or net liquid assets relative to market value — and a firm needs only one of them to be a bargain, whereas the true trap is the firm that offers neither: expensive on earning power and with no realizable asset backing.
evaluated.reasoning: Every construction in this archive has been conjunctive, so the substitutability of earning-power value and asset-backed value has never been tested, and the disjunction defines the short leg as glamour-priced firms with no balance-sheet floor — an economically sharper trap definition than "cheap but illiquid". It is not an aggregation-operator swap on the incumbent inputs because the second leg is deliberately price-scaled net liquid assets, the characteristic that carried the archive's largest standalone alpha, and MAX makes the two legs alternatives rather than joint requirements.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Collected profit claims yield with solvency
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Investors should price the profit the firm has actually collected, not the profit it has booked: gross profit less the increase in operating working capital is the portion of margin converted into settled claims rather than into receivables and inventory, and cheapness measured on that collected profit separates genuine bargains from firms whose apparent earning power is sitting in a warehouse.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not the EBITDA substitution: the numerator is redefined by accrual conversion rather than by which operating expenses are deducted, so the earnings-quality dimension is built into the multiple instead of being applied as an external screen — a distinction the archive can now test, since the accrual channel used as a separate conditioner produced a strong slope (4.63) but no alpha (1.1%). Working capital is computed net of cash and short-term debt so that cash accumulation is not misread as poor collection, and the solvency conditioner is held fixed so the comparison against the incumbent is interpretable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Coverage-ratio conditioned claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(act, lt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What protects a cheap, profitable firm is the multiple by which its liquid resources cover its obligations, not the size of that surplus relative to its asset base; expressing the screen as a coverage ratio judges a small, liquid firm and a large, liquid firm by the same solvency standard.
evaluated.reasoning: The incumbent conditioner (act−lt)/at mechanically rewards firms with small total assets, which is why the critic repeatedly argued it is an asset-lightness proxy rather than a solvency measure; act/lt removes total assets entirely, so if the alpha survives the mechanism is genuinely creditor coverage. It is the single most informative variant to run before the final generation because it determines whether the headline signal should be framed as a solvency screen or an asset-composition tilt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Doubly cheap on profit and liquid assets
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The strongest mispricing occurs where both routes to value point the same way: the firm is cheap relative to its profit stream and the market is simultaneously paying little for a balance sheet whose liquid assets already exceed all obligations.
evaluated.reasoning: The disjunctive MAX version of exactly these two legs earned 2.9% alpha at t 2.31, establishing that the two routes are partly substitutable; the conjunctive version is untested and asks the opposite question, whether requiring both simultaneously concentrates the mispricing further. Price-scaled net liquid assets is the characteristic behind the archive's largest standalone alpha, so pairing it conjunctively with the value leg that supplies the cross-sectional slope is the natural end-point of that line.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Operating runway conditioned claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), cogs), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Survival is a matter of time, not of ratios: the relevant question for a cheap firm is how many years of its own operating cost base its net liquid resources could fund, because that is the horizon over which it can withstand a demand shock without returning to capital markets.
evaluated.reasoning: Scaling the net liquid buffer by an annual flow rather than by assets or liabilities produces a runway measured in years, a conditioner that is structurally incapable of being an asset-lightness proxy and that treats a capital-intensive but cash-covered firm as safe. This is the one genuinely new conditioner concept remaining, and because cogs is already in the value leg's numerator the two legs share accounting inputs in a way that ties survival capacity directly to the profit stream being priced.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Low-leverage conditioned claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(lt, at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The screen that works may be nothing more than low leverage: a cheap, profitable firm that owes little relative to what it owns has both the staying power and the equity claim on any recovery, regardless of whether its assets happen to be current.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the third and simplest partition of the incumbent conditioner, and it is the only one that does not require current assets to be reported, which lifts coverage from 0.121 back toward 0.14 and mechanically improves the precision of the alpha estimate if the economics are unchanged. A result close to the incumbent would mean the archive's entire asset-side story reduces to leverage, which is the most parsimonious and most implementable conclusion available for the final generation.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash-quality conditioned claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(che, act), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Not all current assets are equally real: among cheap, profitable firms the safe ones hold their working capital as cash, while those whose current assets are mostly receivables and inventory hold claims that can be written down or discounted exactly when the business deteriorates.
evaluated.reasoning: This conditions on composition *within* current assets rather than on the current-versus-fixed split, so it is not an affine transform of the archived asset-light screen and it can rank two firms with identical act/at very differently. It tests a distinct economic claim — that the liquidity screen works because of realizability rather than asset-lightness — which the existing archive cannot answer and which matters for choosing the final headline signal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Through-cycle solvency conditioned claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 5), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The relevant solvency standard is the firm's worst position over a full cycle, not its current one: a cheap firm whose net liquid assets stayed positive even at its five-year trough has demonstrated it can absorb a downturn, whereas one that is liquid today only because it recently raised capital or sold assets has not.
evaluated.reasoning: Taking the five-year minimum is a downside-resilience concept rather than a smoothing device — it deliberately ignores good years and scores each firm on its stress point, which is how creditors and distressed-equity investors actually judge staying power. It also separates firms whose current liquidity is a transient consequence of financing activity from those with a durable policy, a distinction the incumbent snapshot screen and any moving average both miss.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash-covered claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap, profitable firm is safe when its cash alone covers a meaningful fraction of everything it owes, because cash is the only asset a creditor cannot dispute; the discount on such a firm cannot be a distress forecast.
evaluated.reasoning: Cash scaled by obligations reads the cash channel as creditor protection rather than as working-capital quality, and it is the direct cash-only analogue of the act/lt coverage screen that produced 3.9% alpha, so comparing the two isolates how much of coverage's value came from the cash component alone. It is also the only cash specification in this batch whose denominator is a claim, which makes it interpretable alongside Signal 1 as protection-versus-composition.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Net-cash conditioned claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash borrowed is not cash owned: a cheap, profitable firm whose cash exceeds its total debt has genuinely unencumbered resources, while a firm holding cash raised from lenders has already pledged that liquidity and remains a trap.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests whether the cash channel is about gross liquidity or about a financing-adjusted position, a distinction the archive has never resolved on the asset side and which matters because gross cash balances are partly mechanical for levered firms with revolver draws. It is the strictest cash specification available and cannot be an affine transform of any prior screen, since it combines an asset item with both debt items.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash-and-coverage conditioned claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(che, act), RATIO(act, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The two surviving forms of balance-sheet quality are logically complementary: cash share of current assets says the working capital is real, and current assets over liabilities says there is enough of it to meet obligations; a cheap, profitable firm needs both to be a bargain rather than a trap.
evaluated.reasoning: These are the two best-performing conditioners from the decomposition (6.3% and 3.9% alpha, with the second also delivering the highest FMB slope of 5.56 and a 0.57 Sharpe), and unlike the gen-6 pairing of liquidity with capital productivity they are not mechanically linked through the same asset-composition identity — one is a quality ratio within current assets, the other a quantity ratio against claims. This is the natural consolidation candidate for the final headline signal if both channels carry independent information.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash runway conditioned claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(che, cogs), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The cash that matters is measured in time: a cheap, profitable firm holding several years of its own operating costs in cash can outlast any downturn without diluting shareholders, whereas one holding weeks of costs must transact at distressed prices.
evaluated.reasoning: The flow-scaled version of the *net liquid asset* buffer delivered only 1.8% alpha, so if the cash-specific runway performs far better, the evidence points to cash rather than to the horizon concept, cleanly separating the two ideas that the gen-8 runway test conflated. Scaling by an annual cost flow also makes this the one cash screen structurally immune to the asset-lightness confound that the critic raised against every balance-sheet-scaled conditioner.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash-quality value on cash-adjusted claims
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(lt, che))), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(che, act), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash should be credited once, not twice: pricing gross profit against market equity plus liabilities net of cash gives the correct claim base, and the cash-share screen should then still separate firms whose remaining working capital is realizable from those whose is not.
evaluated.reasoning: The leader's 6.3% alpha could partly reflect cash entering twice — implicitly through a lower effective claim base and explicitly through the conditioner — and this specification removes that redundancy so the two legs make logically independent statements. It is the integrity check the final recommendation needs: if the alpha survives, the cash-quality mechanism is robust to how the multiple treats cash; if it collapses, the headline result should be reported as a cash-richness valuation effect rather than a working-capital quality screen.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Low working-capital bloat claims value
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, che), revt)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The trap among cheap, profitable firms is operating bloat measured in time: a firm carrying many months of revenue in receivables and inventory has profits sitting in warehouses and unpaid invoices, while a firm needing little non-cash working capital per dollar of revenue is collecting what it books and its low multiple is a mispricing.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a denominator swap on the winning cash screen: deflating non-cash current assets by revenue rather than by current assets converts a composition share into a days-of-sales bloat measure, so two firms with identical cash-to-current-asset ratios are ranked differently according to how much working capital their revenue actually requires. Together with the accepted cash-runway and cash-coverage tests it settles the decisive interpretive question left by the archive's best result — whether the mechanism is the *presence of cash* or the *absence of unrealized operating balances* — which determines how the final headline signal should be described and implemented.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Accrual-signed book-to-market
considered.expression: SUB(MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), 0)), MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 0)))
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness predicts returns only when reported earnings are cash-backed; when accruals are positive (earnings exceed operating cash flow), low price reflects deteriorating fundamentals and cheapness is a trap.
considered.reasoning: The indicator switch gives the same book-to-market rank a positive loading for negative-accrual (clean) firms and a negative loading for positive-accrual (aggressive) firms, so the long-short spread is explicitly cheap-clean minus cheap-dirty rather than a value tilt. This is a conditional sign-flip interaction, not an additive value or accrual factor, because a value-neutral firm receives no exposure regardless of accrual quality.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with improving profitability
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(TREND(RATIO(oancf, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Value pays when the fundamental trajectory is turning up; the multiplicative interaction of high book-to-market and a rising cash-flow-on-assets trend isolates recovering cheap firms from secularly declining ones.
considered.reasoning: A product of within-month ranks scores highly only when both cheapness and a positive multi-year cash profitability trend are present, and it drives to zero if either leg fails, which is the defining feature of an interaction rather than a sum. Using the five-year trend in operating cash flow to assets captures improving earnings quality as a state variable that the market updates slowly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Industry-neutral stable cash value
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ADJ(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), VOL(RATIO(ib, at), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: Within an industry, firms that are cheap relative to peers and simultaneously generate high cash flow with low earnings volatility relative to peers are mispriced, since industry-level valuation and quality differences reflect business models rather than mispricing.
considered.reasoning: Industry demeaning of both legs removes the sector composition that normally makes cheap-and-low-quality portfolios load on a few distressed industries, sharpening the firm-level quality-value contrast. The quality leg nets cash profitability against ROA volatility so that stable cash generators, not merely high-cash-flow cyclicals, are paired with peer-relative cheapness.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Persistent-profit cash flow yield
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MA(oancf, 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(ib, 0), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: A high smoothed operating cash flow yield signals mispricing only when the firm has a demonstrated record of profitable years; the same cash yield in a firm that has lost money in most of the last five years reflects a decaying franchise and is a value trap.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the volatility denominator with a bounded count of profitable years removes the internal inconsistency the critic identified: loss-making, erratic firms can no longer be pulled toward zero and ranked above stable earners, and no 1/volatility term can dominate the cross-section because the conditioning variable is a discrete 0-5 persistence score. The multiplicative rank form means cheapness earns exposure only in proportion to realized profit persistence, so neither leg alone reproduces the ordering.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash-converting EBITDA yield
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che)))), RANK(RATIO(oancf, ebitda)))
considered.hypothesis: A low enterprise-value multiple is informative only when reported EBITDA actually converts into operating cash; when cash conversion is weak, the cheap multiple reflects non-cash accounting profit and working-capital absorption rather than mispricing.
considered.reasoning: This drops the additive three-anomaly stack and replaces it with a single conditioning relationship in which the valuation metric (EBITDA/EV) and the quality metric (oancf/EBITDA) share the same accounting object, so the quality leg directly validates the numerator of the value leg. The product of ranks gives near-zero exposure whenever conversion is poor or the multiple is unattractive, and firms with negative EBITDA are pushed to the bottom of both legs, which is the economically correct treatment.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Gross-profit yield net of obligations
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(re, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Deep value measured in gross profit rather than raw sales already screens out unprofitable revenue, and it converts into realized returns only for firms whose accumulated retained earnings exceed their debt obligations; cheap firms with retained-earnings deficits financed by debt are the archetypal value trap.

considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), 1)))
