considered.reasoning: The conditioner now implements the accrual definition the hypothesis actually requires — cash is netted out of current assets and short-term debt out of current liabilities, so hoarding cash is no longer scored as poor accrual quality and borrowing short is no longer rewarded. Computing accruals from the balance sheet also preserves the 0.12+ coverage that every oancf-based design destroyed, letting the archive finally evaluate the earnings-quality channel named in the theme statement, interacted with the claims-based value leg rather than in isolation.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Solvency and productivity conditioned claims yield
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), SUB(at, act)))))
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness on gross profit relative to all claims converts into return when the firm is both able to survive the wait (current assets covering liabilities) and running its fixed capital productively; these are separate defects — a liquid firm with idle plant and an illiquid firm with productive plant are both traps for different reasons.
considered.reasoning: The archive's two best conditioners deliver alphas of 4.5% and 3.4% through economically different channels, and combining them as a SUMRANK composite before the conjunction avoids the long-leg thinning and instability that a triple-nested MIN would cause. If this beats both parents on alpha and t-statistic the two quality defects are genuinely independent; if it lands between them they are proxies for the same asset-composition effect, which is the key structural question for the final generations.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Peer-relative capital productivity value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), SUB(at, act)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Gross profit per dollar of fixed capital is set largely by industry technology, so the informative signal is a cheap firm whose plant earns more than its own peers' plant, not one that happens to operate in an intrinsically asset-light sector.
considered.reasoning: The productivity conditioner is the most likely of the working channels to be a sector tilt — utilities and heavy manufacturers sit permanently at the bottom — and industry-demeaning only that leg is the sharpest test of whether the 3.4% alpha is firm-level mispricing or sector composition. This matters for the final generations because a sector-driven result would argue for neutralizing the conditioner, while a surviving alpha would justify pushing the productivity channel harder.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Net-debt claims yield with liquid backing
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che))), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Only net financial debt is a hard claim that can force a cheap firm into distress, so measuring cheapness against market equity plus net debt — while separately requiring liquid backing — should identify mispricing more cleanly than treating renewable trade payables as claims.
considered.reasoning: The archive left the claim-definition question genuinely unresolved: total liabilities in the denominator produced the best joint result, yet the trade-float gap showed a 2.4% alpha specifically for firms whose payables are large relative to net debt, and the two findings cannot both be fully right. Holding the conditioner fixed and changing only the claim definition inside the winning recipe settles which liabilities make cheapness dangerous, and it also removes the double liability penalty the critic identified in the current best signal.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Float-financed claims value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), lt), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Among cheap, profitable firms the safe ones are those whose obligations are mostly supplier and operating liabilities rather than borrowings, because trade creditors monitor continuously and roll their exposure while lenders can accelerate at exactly the wrong moment.
considered.reasoning: The liability-composition channel produced a strong slope but null alpha when paired with a raw sales-yield value leg in gen 3, whereas the same economics priced as a valuation gap produced a 2.4% alpha with a null slope in gen 5 — pairing it with the value leg now known to carry the cross-sectional signal is the natural test of whether both halves can be obtained at once. It also diversifies the batch away from asset-side conditioners toward the liability side, so the generation as a whole covers both sources of trap risk.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with improving capital utilization
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), SUB(at, act)), 5), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: What distinguishes a mispriced cheap firm from a trap is not only how productive its plant is today but whether that productivity is rising: a cheap firm extracting steadily more gross profit from the same fixed capital base is filling capacity that the market still prices as idle, whereas a cheap firm with falling capital productivity is losing share and its discount will keep widening.
considered.reasoning: This changes the economic content rather than the operator: the archive established that the *level* of fixed-capital productivity carries alpha, and the untested question is whether the market misprices the level or the direction of change, which is a different behavioural claim about slow updating of capacity expectations. The five-year trend is genuinely slow-moving and orthogonal to the level for many firms — a low-productivity plant can be improving fast — so the result is informative regardless of sign and cannot be replicated by the accepted Signal 1's static composite.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Profit yield on illiquid claim base
considered.expression: RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(lt, act))), 1))
considered.hypothesis: The economically relevant capital a buyer must fund is market equity plus the liabilities that current assets cannot already extinguish; pricing gross profit against that net, illiquid claim base means a firm whose receivables, inventory and cash already offset its obligations is recognised as cheap, while a firm whose liabilities exceed its liquid resources is correctly recognised as expensive.
considered.reasoning: The flow-plus-stock addition that made the earlier version arbitrarily weighted is removed: the numerator is now purely a flow and the balance-sheet quality information enters as a deduction inside the denominator, so all terms in the claim base are stocks and no implicit capitalization multiple is assumed. It is distinct from gross-profits-to-enterprise-value, which nets only cash, and it makes the solvency conditioner that produced the archive's 4.5% alpha part of the multiple itself; the rare cases where current assets exceed market equity plus liabilities are the deep net-net names and are handled by winsorizing before ranking.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Two-sided balance-sheet quality value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), lt))))
considered.hypothesis: A cheap, profitable firm avoids the trap for two logically separate reasons: its assets are liquid enough to cover its obligations, and the obligations it has are renewable supplier float rather than acceleratable debt. Asset-side capacity and liability-side patience are distinct forms of staying power.
considered.reasoning: The gen-6 attempt to combine two conditioners paired asset liquidity with capital productivity, which the critic correctly noted are mechanically linked through the same small non-current asset base; pairing asset liquidity with liability *composition* combines channels that were separately alpha-positive (4.5% and 3.0%) and are not driven by the same accounting identity. This is the last remaining plausible route to independent, additive quality information within the winning recipe.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Smoothed earnings power on claims with solvency
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(SUB(sale, cogs), 3), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The cheapness that matters is measured against normal earning power, not against a single year's gross profit: averaging three years of gross profit removes cyclical peaks that make deteriorating firms look cheap and cyclical troughs that hide genuinely cheap franchises.
considered.reasoning: Every value leg in this archive has used a single fiscal year, so the timing of the earnings-power measurement is an untested design dimension, and it targets a specific trap mechanism — peak-earnings cheapness — that the balance-sheet conditioners cannot detect. Smoothing should also reduce annual turnover in the long leg, which is the most likely source of incremental improvement in ls_talpha given the alpha magnitude is already established.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Peer-relative claims value with solvency
considered.expression: MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Gross-profit multiples differ permanently across industries, so the mispriced firm is the one cheap relative to its own peers, while the solvency requirement remains an absolute standard because creditors do not grade on an industry curve.
considered.reasoning: Industry-demeaning the productivity conditioner destroyed its alpha, which showed the conditioner side is a sector effect; the complementary and unanswered question is whether the *value* leg's contribution is within-industry mispricing or a cross-industry multiple tilt, and this signal isolates exactly that by demeaning only the value leg. The answer determines whether the final consolidated signal should be industry-neutral on the valuation dimension, which materially affects the stability of the long-short spread.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Earned-buffer claims value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(re, lt), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The deepest form of staying power is a stock of profits already earned and retained relative to what the firm owes: such a firm has demonstrated over its life that it can fund obligations internally, whereas a cheap firm with an accumulated deficit against heavy liabilities has never demonstrated it and its discount is a distress forecast.
considered.reasoning: All the alpha-producing conditioners so far measure current asset or liability composition; retained earnings relative to liabilities is a cumulative, history-based buffer that is conceptually distinct — asset-heavy old firms with decades of retained profit can score highly here while failing every liquidity screen. Because it uses no price term and no flow, it cannot double-count the value leg or the asset-lightness tilt, making it the most genuinely new conditioner class available within the winning recipe.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Two-route value disjunction
considered.expression: MAX(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: There are two independent routes by which a stock can be worth more than its price — a large profit stream relative to all claims, or net liquid assets relative to market value — and a firm needs only one of them to be a bargain, whereas the true trap is the firm that offers neither: expensive on earning power and with no realizable asset backing.
considered.reasoning: Every construction in this archive has been conjunctive, so the substitutability of earning-power value and asset-backed value has never been tested, and the disjunction defines the short leg as glamour-priced firms with no balance-sheet floor — an economically sharper trap definition than "cheap but illiquid". It is not an aggregation-operator swap on the incumbent inputs because the second leg is deliberately price-scaled net liquid assets, the characteristic that carried the archive's largest standalone alpha, and MAX makes the two legs alternatives rather than joint requirements.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Collected profit claims yield with solvency
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Investors should price the profit the firm has actually collected, not the profit it has booked: gross profit less the increase in operating working capital is the portion of margin converted into settled claims rather than into receivables and inventory, and cheapness measured on that collected profit separates genuine bargains from firms whose apparent earning power is sitting in a warehouse.
considered.reasoning: This is not the EBITDA substitution: the numerator is redefined by accrual conversion rather than by which operating expenses are deducted, so the earnings-quality dimension is built into the multiple instead of being applied as an external screen — a distinction the archive can now test, since the accrual channel used as a separate conditioner produced a strong slope (4.63) but no alpha (1.1%). Working capital is computed net of cash and short-term debt so that cash accumulation is not misread as poor collection, and the solvency conditioner is held fixed so the comparison against the incumbent is interpretable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Coverage-ratio conditioned claims value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(act, lt), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: What protects a cheap, profitable firm is the multiple by which its liquid resources cover its obligations, not the size of that surplus relative to its asset base; expressing the screen as a coverage ratio judges a small, liquid firm and a large, liquid firm by the same solvency standard.
considered.reasoning: The incumbent conditioner (act−lt)/at mechanically rewards firms with small total assets, which is why the critic repeatedly argued it is an asset-lightness proxy rather than a solvency measure; act/lt removes total assets entirely, so if the alpha survives the mechanism is genuinely creditor coverage. It is the single most informative variant to run before the final generation because it determines whether the headline signal should be framed as a solvency screen or an asset-composition tilt.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Doubly cheap on profit and liquid assets
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The strongest mispricing occurs where both routes to value point the same way: the firm is cheap relative to its profit stream and the market is simultaneously paying little for a balance sheet whose liquid assets already exceed all obligations.
considered.reasoning: The disjunctive MAX version of exactly these two legs earned 2.9% alpha at t 2.31, establishing that the two routes are partly substitutable; the conjunctive version is untested and asks the opposite question, whether requiring both simultaneously concentrates the mispricing further. Price-scaled net liquid assets is the characteristic behind the archive's largest standalone alpha, so pairing it conjunctively with the value leg that supplies the cross-sectional slope is the natural end-point of that line.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Operating runway conditioned claims value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), cogs), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Survival is a matter of time, not of ratios: the relevant question for a cheap firm is how many years of its own operating cost base its net liquid resources could fund, because that is the horizon over which it can withstand a demand shock without returning to capital markets.
considered.reasoning: Scaling the net liquid buffer by an annual flow rather than by assets or liabilities produces a runway measured in years, a conditioner that is structurally incapable of being an asset-lightness proxy and that treats a capital-intensive but cash-covered firm as safe. This is the one genuinely new conditioner concept remaining, and because cogs is already in the value leg's numerator the two legs share accounting inputs in a way that ties survival capacity directly to the profit stream being priced.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Low-leverage conditioned claims value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(lt, at)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The screen that works may be nothing more than low leverage: a cheap, profitable firm that owes little relative to what it owns has both the staying power and the equity claim on any recovery, regardless of whether its assets happen to be current.
considered.reasoning: This is the third and simplest partition of the incumbent conditioner, and it is the only one that does not require current assets to be reported, which lifts coverage from 0.121 back toward 0.14 and mechanically improves the precision of the alpha estimate if the economics are unchanged. A result close to the incumbent would mean the archive's entire asset-side story reduces to leverage, which is the most parsimonious and most implementable conclusion available for the final generation.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash-quality conditioned claims value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(che, act), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Not all current assets are equally real: among cheap, profitable firms the safe ones hold their working capital as cash, while those whose current assets are mostly receivables and inventory hold claims that can be written down or discounted exactly when the business deteriorates.
considered.reasoning: This conditions on composition *within* current assets rather than on the current-versus-fixed split, so it is not an affine transform of the archived asset-light screen and it can rank two firms with identical act/at very differently. It tests a distinct economic claim — that the liquidity screen works because of realizability rather than asset-lightness — which the existing archive cannot answer and which matters for choosing the final headline signal.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Through-cycle solvency conditioned claims value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 5), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The relevant solvency standard is the firm's worst position over a full cycle, not its current one: a cheap firm whose net liquid assets stayed positive even at its five-year trough has demonstrated it can absorb a downturn, whereas one that is liquid today only because it recently raised capital or sold assets has not.
considered.reasoning: Taking the five-year minimum is a downside-resilience concept rather than a smoothing device — it deliberately ignores good years and scores each firm on its stress point, which is how creditors and distressed-equity investors actually judge staying power. It also separates firms whose current liquidity is a transient consequence of financing activity from those with a durable policy, a distinction the incumbent snapshot screen and any moving average both miss.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash-covered claims value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A cheap, profitable firm is safe when its cash alone covers a meaningful fraction of everything it owes, because cash is the only asset a creditor cannot dispute; the discount on such a firm cannot be a distress forecast.
considered.reasoning: Cash scaled by obligations reads the cash channel as creditor protection rather than as working-capital quality, and it is the direct cash-only analogue of the act/lt coverage screen that produced 3.9% alpha, so comparing the two isolates how much of coverage's value came from the cash component alone. It is also the only cash specification in this batch whose denominator is a claim, which makes it interpretable alongside Signal 1 as protection-versus-composition.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Net-cash conditioned claims value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Cash borrowed is not cash owned: a cheap, profitable firm whose cash exceeds its total debt has genuinely unencumbered resources, while a firm holding cash raised from lenders has already pledged that liquidity and remains a trap.
considered.reasoning: This tests whether the cash channel is about gross liquidity or about a financing-adjusted position, a distinction the archive has never resolved on the asset side and which matters because gross cash balances are partly mechanical for levered firms with revolver draws. It is the strictest cash specification available and cannot be an affine transform of any prior screen, since it combines an asset item with both debt items.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash-and-coverage conditioned claims value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(che, act), RATIO(act, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: The two surviving forms of balance-sheet quality are logically complementary: cash share of current assets says the working capital is real, and current assets over liabilities says there is enough of it to meet obligations; a cheap, profitable firm needs both to be a bargain rather than a trap.
considered.reasoning: These are the two best-performing conditioners from the decomposition (6.3% and 3.9% alpha, with the second also delivering the highest FMB slope of 5.56 and a 0.57 Sharpe), and unlike the gen-6 pairing of liquidity with capital productivity they are not mechanically linked through the same asset-composition identity — one is a quality ratio within current assets, the other a quantity ratio against claims. This is the natural consolidation candidate for the final headline signal if both channels carry independent information.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash runway conditioned claims value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(che, cogs), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The cash that matters is measured in time: a cheap, profitable firm holding several years of its own operating costs in cash can outlast any downturn without diluting shareholders, whereas one holding weeks of costs must transact at distressed prices.
considered.reasoning: The flow-scaled version of the *net liquid asset* buffer delivered only 1.8% alpha, so if the cash-specific runway performs far better, the evidence points to cash rather than to the horizon concept, cleanly separating the two ideas that the gen-8 runway test conflated. Scaling by an annual cost flow also makes this the one cash screen structurally immune to the asset-lightness confound that the critic raised against every balance-sheet-scaled conditioner.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash-quality value on cash-adjusted claims
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(lt, che))), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(che, act), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Cash should be credited once, not twice: pricing gross profit against market equity plus liabilities net of cash gives the correct claim base, and the cash-share screen should then still separate firms whose remaining working capital is realizable from those whose is not.
considered.reasoning: The leader's 6.3% alpha could partly reflect cash entering twice — implicitly through a lower effective claim base and explicitly through the conditioner — and this specification removes that redundancy so the two legs make logically independent statements. It is the integrity check the final recommendation needs: if the alpha survives, the cash-quality mechanism is robust to how the multiple treats cash; if it collapses, the headline result should be reported as a cash-richness valuation effect rather than a working-capital quality screen.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Low working-capital bloat claims value
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, che), revt)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The trap among cheap, profitable firms is operating bloat measured in time: a firm carrying many months of revenue in receivables and inventory has profits sitting in warehouses and unpaid invoices, while a firm needing little non-cash working capital per dollar of revenue is collecting what it books and its low multiple is a mispricing.
considered.reasoning: This is not a denominator swap on the winning cash screen: deflating non-cash current assets by revenue rather than by current assets converts a composition share into a days-of-sales bloat measure, so two firms with identical cash-to-current-asset ratios are ranked differently according to how much working capital their revenue actually requires. Together with the accepted cash-runway and cash-coverage tests it settles the decisive interpretive question left by the archive's best result — whether the mechanism is the *presence of cash* or the *absence of unrealized operating balances* — which determines how the final headline signal should be described and implemented.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: The expression does compute what the hypothesis claims (BM rank signed by accrual sign, so the spread is cheap-clean minus cheap-dirty), but it is close to the documented "accrual anomaly is stronger among value stocks" result and the hard discontinuity at accruals = 0 will make portfolio membership unstable for the many firms with near-zero accruals.

Dividing a signed earnings yield by ROA volatility is internally inconsistent with the stated hypothesis because loss-making firms with erratic earnings get pulled *toward zero* (i.e., ranked better than stable loss-makers), and the signal's cross-sectional variation will be dominated by 1/volatility, effectively rediscovering the low-earnings-volatility/quality effect rather than a conditional value effect.

This is an additive stack of three separately published anomalies (EBITDA/EV, gross profitability, accruals) with no conditioning structure, and the nested SUMRANK does not deliver the claimed equal weighting since the outer rank gives EBITDA/EV roughly double the weight of each quality leg.

The construction is coherent and matches the hypothesis, but a product of two [0,1] ranks is close to a monotone transform of an additive composite, so it is only weakly an interaction and overlaps materially with the published value-plus-improving-fundamentals (Piotroski–So) result.

A sales-to-price value leg screened by retained earnings and leverage is a well-trodden value-trap/financial-strength composite with no conditioning mechanism, and the nested SUMRANK again contradicts the claimed equal weighting of the three channels.

Industry-demeaning both legs is a substantive design choice that plausibly addresses the sector-concentration problem in value-quality spreads, but the quality leg subtracts a volatility from a cash-flow ratio in raw units without standardization, so the effective relative weight of the two components is arbitrary and should be replaced by a rank difference.

The product of two signed z-scores is maximally positive for BOTH cheap-profitable and expensive-unprofitable firms, so the long leg contains exactly the stocks the hypothesis calls overpriced — an internal sign inconsistency — and the underlying value×profitability combination is one of the most heavily published anomaly pairings (Novy-Marx, Asness et al. QMJ, FF5).

This inherits the same double-negative sign pathology as Signal 1 and differs only by swapping ZSCORE for IND_ZSCORE, which is a cosmetic neutralization variant rather than a substantively different mechanism.

Same z-score product defect (expensive plus liability-heavy also scores high, contradicting the value-trap story), and the "cheap plus balance-sheet strength" screen is close to both the archive's retained-earnings-net-of-debt leg and the published Piotroski/distress-screened value literature.

The own-history cheapness percentile crossed with a gross-margin trend is a genuinely fresher construction, but the ZSCORE product again assigns top scores to the low-cheapness/eroding-margin cell that the hypothesis never claims is underpriced, so the expression does not implement the stated two-cell logic.

A defensible and untested capital-consumption channel, though the reviewer should note that since EBITDA−DP=EBIT the rank difference is largely monotone in depreciation-to-market-cap rather than a true within-EBITDA-yield conditional as the reasoning claims, so it risks collapsing into a single capital-intensity characteristic.

The expression does implement what the hypothesis describes — a within-deep-value long-liquid/short-illiquid contrast with cancelling HML loadings — but the hard 1.5 threshold is arbitrary, most low-S/P firms collapse near zero, and the value-plus-financial-strength screen is conceptually adjacent to published Piotroski-style value-trap filters.

critic_notes.target_name: Earned versus contributed equity value gap
critic_notes.rationale: With a common market-value denominator the rank gap is essentially a monotone function of retained earnings relative to book equity, which is a direct rediscovery of the published book-to-market decomposition into retained-earnings and contributed-capital components (Ball, Gerakos, Linnainmaa & Nikolaev), and it also overlaps the archive's gen-0 retained-earnings-versus-debt value signal.

The construction is internally consistent and the continuous conditioning is a genuine improvement over the archive's arbitrary 1.5 current-ratio cut, but the long leg is close to the well-documented Graham net-current-asset-value effect and the numerator is negative for most firms, so the rank gap may end up proxying asset-composition/capital-intensity rather than the intended solvency-backed discount.

Because both legs share the price denominator, the difference collapses to an ordering in gross profits relative to book equity, i.e. essentially Novy-Marx gross profitability combined with gross-profits-to-market — both published — and the gross-profit-to-market leg was already used in the archive's gen-0 signal.

This is the same MIN-of-winsorized-z-scores template as the archive's "Cheapness with stable cost structure" with the quality leg swapped and the sign flipped, and the design is ambiguous because MIN makes the low end a mixture of expensive firms and low-leverage firms while the high end is deep value, so a negative expected slope directly contradicts the value premium unless distress (itself a known anomaly) dominates.

The scale-free conditioner is a defensible, diagnosis-driven response to the gen-1 depreciation gap's collapse into depreciation-to-market-cap rather than a cosmetic variant, though (ebitda-dp)/ebitda is unstable and sign-flipped for negative-EBITDA firms and the MIN template repeats an archive design that already failed.

Operating cash flow already nets out working-capital changes, so subtracting Δ(act−lct) again double-counts, and with a common price denominator the rank gap reduces to minus working-capital accruals scaled by market cap — a direct restatement of the Sloan accruals anomaly rather than the claimed cash-flow-quality interaction.

The expression matches the hypothesis and the sign is unambiguous, and swapping the unstable (ebitda-dp)/ebitda conditioner for a monotone EBIT-to-total-claims coverage ratio is a genuine economic change rather than a cosmetic one — though it should be acknowledged that EBIT/liabilities is close to the Altman/Ohlson distress ingredients and the two legs share a numerator, so the MIN may collapse toward a single scaled-EBIT ordering.

The liability-composition channel is untested in the archive and the construction is internally consistent, but (lct-dlc)/lt is heavily industry-determined (retail/wholesale trade credit) and overlaps the published net-operating-liabilities/accruals channel, so the result risks being a sector tilt rather than the monitoring story claimed.

The diagnosis of the gen-2 liquidation gap is honest and the MIN structure does restore the value tilt, but (act-lt)/at is close to a mechanical restatement of ceq/at minus fixed-asset intensity, so the conditioner is largely a low-leverage/asset-light screen and the combination sits near the well-documented Graham net-current-asset anomaly.

This is the same multiplicative template as the archive's already-failed "Equity-funded sales yield" with the scaling factor swapped for DuPont current-asset turnover, a published efficiency signal, and the unranked product of two heavy-tailed ratios (sales²/(P·act)) will be dominated by whichever leg has the fatter tail rather than by the claimed conjunction.

The post-dividend cash-flow-to-current-liabilities conditioner is a substantively different sustainability test from the gross-profit payout-share version, the rank-product direction is consistent with the positive expected sign, and the main caveats are coverage loss from oancf availability and the fact that the signal is effectively defined only among dividend payers.

(oancf - dp)/market cap is a direct rediscovery of free-cash-flow yield with depreciation as the capex proxy — a single published value ratio with no cross-theme interaction at all — and while its value as a clean diagnostic baseline is arguable, it does not meet the brief for a novel interacted signal.

This is a single-input substitution (che for act) in the archive's "Cheap with liquid asset backing," and because cash almost never exceeds total liabilities, (che−lt)/at collapses into a monotone low-leverage/high-cash proxy — so it will not cleanly adjudicate "solvency backing vs. asset-lightness" as claimed, and it mostly re-tests the known cash-holdings/low-leverage tilt inside value.

The two conditioners are close to mechanically redundant — a high (act−lt)/at essentially requires a small fixed-asset base, which is the same thing as low dp/at — so the stated test of "independent and additive alpha channels" is confounded, and the triple-nested MIN will thin and destabilize the long leg while inheriting a depreciation channel whose archive parent already showed a slope/alpha sign conflict.

Short-term debt relative to liquid assets is a genuinely untested channel here (levels, changes and composition were tested, rollover timing was not), the sign convention via NEG is internally consistent with the positive expected sign, and it keeps balance-sheet-only coverage — though it partially overlaps the archive's "Supplier-financed deep value," which found a strong slope but null alpha, so that null is the most likely outcome to diagnose.

The conditioner is a bounded 0–5 count with almost all mass at 0 and 5, so under MIN the signal degenerates into "gross-profit yield among consistent payers, with all non-payers tied at the floor" — producing a huge tied short leg that is effectively the well-documented dividend-payer/quality screen rather than a continuous trap-vs-bargain conditioner.

Internally consistent and reasonably motivated as a flow-side counterpart to the failed deleveraging conditioner, but the five-year trend in re/at is arithmetically close to average retained ROA, so this sits uncomfortably near the well-known value×profitability (and retained-earnings-to-market) combination and risks being largely spanned by RMW.

This is a one-operator robustness variant of the archive's "Cheap with liquid asset backing" (IND_ZSCORE swapped for ZSCORE on the conditioner) — a legitimate diagnostic but not a substantively new signal, and it is also redundant with the two other liquidity-conditioner variants submitted in this same batch.

critic_notes.target_name: Claims-based profit yield free of fixed capital
critic_notes.rationale: The composite is internally consistent (asset-heaviness per dollar of price enters negatively, matching the hypothesis) and SUMRANK avoids the mechanical degeneracy that a MIN of two ME-scaled legs would create, but the stated diagnosis is only half right — one of the two large archive alphas came from depreciation-to-price, not non-current-assets-to-price — and the fixed-capital leg carried a negative FMB slope, so the two channels may fight cross-sectionally.

Swapping the value leg from book-to-market to the claims-based gross-profit yield while holding the liquidity conditioner fixed is a legitimate one-variable test of whether the HML loading or the solvency screen drives the archive's only both-positive result, though it remains an incremental recombination of two already-evaluated legs and risks double-penalizing liabilities (in the denominator and again via act−lt).

Both legs scale by market equity in opposite directions — low price raises leg 1 and pushes leg 2 more negative — so MIN will be pinned to the fixed-capital leg for exactly the cheap firms the hypothesis targets, making the signal largely a rescaled rediscovery of the archive's Liquidation-backed value gap rather than a clean horse race.

Subtracting dp from the numerator of an already-evaluated archive expression is a near-cosmetic single-term tweak, and the resulting construct (post-depreciation operating profit over market equity plus liabilities) is essentially the published enterprise-multiple/profits-to-EV anomaly.

The economic question (which liabilities actually make cheapness dangerous) is real and unsettled in the archive, but the expression is gross-profits-to-enterprise-value — a standard, widely documented valuation multiple — and is only a denominator substitution on an already-evaluated signal.

The conditioner does not compute what the hypothesis describes: Δ(act−lct) includes changes in cash and short-term debt, so cash accumulation is scored as bad accruals and short-term borrowing as good, and the underlying accrual channel is the canonical Sloan anomaly rather than a novel interaction — netting che and dlc out of working capital would be the minimum fix.

critic_notes.target_name: Solvency and productivity conditioned claims yield
critic_notes.rationale: A coherent and explicitly diagnostic combination of the archive's two best conditioners, but the two legs are mechanically linked (both load on a small non-current asset base, since (act−lt)/at rises and (at−act) falls together), so a SUMRANK is likely to double-count one asset-composition tilt rather than combine independent defects — the test is worth running but the null-hypothesis outcome is the more probable one.

By the proposer's own admission this holds economic content identical to Signal 1 and varies only MIN versus rank-product, which is precisely the cosmetic operator variant the objective warns against, and generic three-way rank products are a well-worn construction unlikely to yield new economic insight.

Industry-demeaning only the productivity leg is a substantively motivated and interpretable test of whether the 3.4% alpha is firm-level mispricing or a persistent asset-intensity sector tilt, and either outcome gives actionable guidance.

critic_notes.target_name: Net-debt claims yield with liquid backing
critic_notes.rationale: Changing only the claim definition inside the winning recipe is the right way to settle the unresolved payables-versus-debt question, though the proposer should watch for cash-rich firms driving the denominator toward or below zero, which can flip the ratio's sign and contaminate the extreme deciles despite 1% winsorization.

critic_notes.target_name: Earnings power plus liquid backing to price
critic_notes.rationale: The numerator adds an annual flow (gross profit) to a balance-sheet stock (net current assets minus all liabilities) with no capitalization multiple, so the implicit weighting is arbitrary and the signal will be dominated by whichever term has larger typical scale — and what remains is close to a mechanical blend of Graham NCAV/net-net value and gross profitability, both published anomalies.

Re-pairing the liability-composition channel with the value leg that actually carries the cross-sectional slope is a legitimate and diversifying test, but (lct−dlc)/lt is itself tilted toward low-debt, short-duration-balance-sheet firms and therefore only partly independent of the asset-side conditioners already shown to work, so the incremental information may be small.

Pairing the two independently alpha-positive conditioners (liquid backing and operating-liability composition) is internally consistent and less mechanically redundant than the gen-6 productivity pairing, but the two legs are partly in accounting tension (large lct depresses act−lt), so the incremental information may be small and the design remains a modest re-shuffle of existing archive components.

This is a pure aggregation-operator swap (MIN→SUMRANK) on the exact same two inputs as the archive's incumbent "Liquid-backed claims profit yield", i.e. the cosmetic variant the objective explicitly warns against, and the archive already demonstrates the additive form works for a different pair.

critic_notes.target_name: Smoothed earnings power on claims with solvency
critic_notes.rationale: Three-year averaging of the numerator is a genuinely untested measurement-window dimension aimed at a specific trap channel (peak-earnings cheapness) rather than a re-sorted conditioner, though it is a familiar normalized-earnings idea and will cost coverage and dilute cross-sectional dispersion.

Gross profit over market equity plus total liabilities replaced by EBITDA is close to the published enterprise-multiple (EV/EBITDA) anomaly, and the proposal is otherwise a single numerator substitution into the incumbent structure — a diagnostic ablation rather than a new mechanism.

Industry-demeaning only the valuation leg while keeping solvency absolute is an internally coherent and informative decomposition of where the incumbent's alpha originates, though industry-relative value is itself well documented and the change is a single-operator substitution.

Retained earnings scaled by total liabilities is a genuinely different, stock-based and price-free conditioner class that cannot mechanically duplicate the value leg or the asset-lightness tilt, and while it echoes an Altman-Z component and a gen-0 term, its use as a conditioner on the claims-based gross-profit yield is untested here.

The act/lt conditioner is not a monotone transform of the incumbent (act−lt)/at screen and cleanly separates creditor-coverage from asset-lightness, so the diagnostic is legitimate even if the construction is only one denominator away from an existing archive entry.

ZSCORE(WINSOR(act/at)) is an affine transform of ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG((at−act)/at))), so this is a mathematically identical rediscovery of the archived "Cheap and asset-light on the balance sheet" signal (fmb 4.653, alpha 0.037).

critic_notes.target_name: Doubly cheap on profit and liquid assets
critic_notes.rationale: MIN of the two legs asks a genuinely different (conjunctive) question than the archived MAX disjunction and uses a price-scaled buffer rather than the asset-scaled one, though it is a modest step and likely highly correlated with the existing 0.045-alpha liquid-backed variant.

Scaling the net liquid buffer by an annual cost flow yields a horizon-based survival screen that is structurally immune to the asset-lightness confound criticized in the incumbent, making this the most substantively new conditioner in the batch; the only caveat is that 1/cogs partly reintroduces a size/turnover tilt.

A three-year moving average of the identical incumbent conditioner is a cosmetic smoothing variant whose stated motivation (fiscal-year-end window dressing of liquidity) is weakly connected to annual balance-sheet data and is unlikely to change the economic story.

Book-equity-to-assets as the screen is a defensible parsimony test that also lifts coverage, but note it is a monotone transform of (at−lt)/at and thus close in spirit to the archived equity-funded value work, and its overlap with the lt already in the value denominator means a positive result will be hard to interpret as independent.

che/at is mechanically the product of two conditioners the archive has already tested separately (che/act at 6.3% and current-asset intensity implicit in the 3.7% asset-lightness screen), so it is a denominator swap whose likely outcome is already interpolable and adds little independent information.

Scaling cash by total obligations is a coherent creditor-protection reading that decomposes the act/lt coverage result into its cash component, though it is arithmetically the product of the two conditioners in Signals 1 and 4 and so is only partially independent of this same batch.

Netting total debt against cash is a substantively new financing-adjusted liquidity conditioner that no archive screen spans, and it addresses a real confound (revolver-funded cash balances), with only mild overlap risk against the already-tested low-leverage screen.

Consolidating the two best conditioners is a defensible headline candidate, but the claim of independence is overstated since che/act times act/lt is exactly Signal 2's ratio, and SUMRANK averaging risks diluting the 6.3% leader rather than improving it.

Replacing net liquid assets with cash in the already-tested cogs-scaled runway is a clean numerator-versus-denominator disambiguation and is genuinely immune to the asset-composition confound, though it remains a one-term substitution on an existing specification.

This is the most valuable proposal in the batch because it directly tests whether the leader's alpha is double-counting cash in both the valuation multiple and the conditioner, and either outcome changes how the headline result should be interpreted.
